Contents.Title: Introduction: Sign Up
Contents.Contents:
We Already Built the Sign-In

Welcome to the next part of our Website Development project.

In the previous section, we built a basic Sign-In system.

We learned how JavaScript can:

  • find HTML elements using IDs
  • listen for form submission
  • read values from inputs
  • store values in variables
  • compare values
  • use if and else to make decisions
  • display a result on the webpage

We also created the Sign-Up interface earlier while learning HTML and CSS.

That means the Sign-Up form already has a visual structure waiting for us.

However, there is an important difference:

Sign-In
↓
HTML exists
↓
CSS exists
↓
JavaScript functionality exists

Sign-Up
↓
HTML exists
↓
CSS exists
↓
JavaScript functionality comes next

Why Do We Need Sign Up?

So far, our Login example assumed that an account already existed.

But a real application can have many different users.

We cannot expect every person to use one fixed account.

Users need a way to create their own accounts.

That process is called Sign Up, also commonly called registration.

The basic idea is:

Sign Up
↓
User provides account information
↓
Application stores the account
↓
Later, Login can check that account

Our Sign-Up Interface Already Exists

You already created the Sign-Up HTML and CSS earlier in the course.

Before continuing, look at your existing project.

You should already have something similar to:

Sign-In
├── Email
├── Password
└── Login button

Sign-Up
├── Name
├── Email
├── Password
├── Confirm Password
└── Sign Up button

You do not need to throw away the project or create another webpage.

We are continuing the same project and adding behavior to the Sign-Up interface that already exists.

Try It

Open the project you built in the previous lessons. Look at your existing Sign-Up interface and make sure you can switch between the Sign-In and Sign-Up views using the HTML and CSS you already created. You are welcome to use what you already built instead of recreating the interface from the beginning.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Why We Need More Than One Variable
Contents.Contents:
One Variable Can Store One Value

In our Login lesson, we worked with variables such as:

const email = "student@example.com";
const password = "1234";

This works well when we are dealing with one piece of information at a time.

But Sign-Up introduces a new problem.

Imagine that five people create accounts.

User 1
Name: Alex
Email: alex@example.com
Password: example123

User 2
Name: Jamie
Email: jamie@example.com
Password: hello123

User 3
Name: Sam
Email: sam@example.com
Password: password123

We could create separate variables for everything, but that would quickly become difficult to organize.

const name1 = "Alex";
const email1 = "alex@example.com";
const password1 = "example123";

const name2 = "Jamie";
const email2 = "jamie@example.com";
const password2 = "hello123";

What if there were 100 users?

We need better ways to organize related information.

Two Important JavaScript Data Structures

JavaScript gives us structures that allow us to organize collections of information.

Two especially important ones for our project are:

Array
↓
Store multiple items

Object
↓
Store named pieces of information

Once we understand these two structures, we can combine them to represent many users.

The Goal

Eventually, we want to be able to represent information like this:

Many users
↓
Each user has information
↓
Array stores the users
↓
Object describes each user

Before we build that combination, we need to understand each structure separately.

Try It

Before moving on, think about the difference between storing one value and storing many related values. This distinction will become important when we begin creating multiple accounts.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Introduction to Arrays
Contents.Contents:
What Is an Array?

An array is a JavaScript value that can store multiple values in an ordered collection.

Instead of creating many separate variables, we can place multiple related items inside one array.

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

Here, fruits is one variable, but it contains three values.

You can think of an array like a row of storage slots.

[ "Apple", "Banana", "Orange" ]
    ↓       ↓        ↓
  item 0  item 1   item 2

Why Would We Use an Array?

Imagine we want to keep track of several products:

const products = [
  "Burger",
  "Pizza",
  "Fries",
  "Hotdog"
];

Instead of creating a separate variable for every product, one array contains them all.

This becomes extremely useful when a program needs to work with a collection of items.

Arrays Use Square Brackets

Array values are written inside square brackets:

[ ]

The individual values are separated by commas.

["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"]

Reading an Array Item

We can read an item by using its index.

An index is the position of an item inside the array.

JavaScript arrays start counting at 0.

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

console.log(fruits[0]);
console.log(fruits[1]);
console.log(fruits[2]);

The results are:

Apple
Banana
Orange

Why Does It Start at 0?

This is an important JavaScript rule.

Index 0 → first item
Index 1 → second item
Index 2 → third item

So the index is not the same as the human way of counting items.

Using console.log()

We can use console.log() to inspect individual array items.

console.log(fruits[1]);

This lets us see exactly which item JavaScript is retrieving.

How Many Items Are There?

Arrays have a length property.

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

console.log(fruits.length);

The result is:

3

Notice that the length is 3 while the last index is 2.

That is because the array has three items, but counting the indexes starts at 0.

Adding a New Item

JavaScript provides the push() method for adding a new item to the end of an array.

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana"];

fruits.push("Orange");

The array now contains:

["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"]

The array has grown from two items to three.

Arrays Can Grow and Shrink

JavaScript arrays are dynamic. Their size can change while the program is running.

We can add items:

fruits.push("Mango");

And we can remove items.

For example, pop() removes the last item:

fruits.pop();

The array can therefore grow or shrink as our program needs.

Removing an Item

Another useful method is splice().

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

fruits.splice(1, 1);

The first number tells JavaScript where to start.

The second number tells JavaScript how many items to remove.

After this example, the array becomes:

["Apple", "Orange"]

Editing an Item

We can replace an item by assigning a new value to its index.

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

fruits[1] = "Mango";

The array is now:

["Apple", "Mango", "Orange"]

We used the index to tell JavaScript exactly which item should change.

Why Arrays Matter for Our Project

Eventually, Sign Up will need to handle more than one account.

An array gives us a place where many accounts can be stored:

const users = [
  ...many users...
];

We are not creating the user system yet. We are first learning the structure that will make it possible.

Try It

Create an array of your favorite fruits. Read individual items using indexes. Print the array length with .length. Add an item using push(). Remove the last item using pop(). Remove an item using splice(). Finally, replace one item by assigning a new value to its index.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Introduction to Objects
Contents.Contents:
What Is an Object?

We now know how an array stores multiple values.

But sometimes we need to store several pieces of information about one thing.

For example, a customer might have:

Name
Email
Age
Address

Putting those values into an ordinary array is possible, but it does not clearly tell us what each value means.

["Alex", "alex@example.com", 18, "Davao"]

Which value is the email?

Which value is the age?

A better structure for this situation is an object.

Object or Dictionary?

You may hear this kind of structure called a dictionary in other programming languages.

In JavaScript, the usual name is object.

For this course, we may describe it as a dictionary-like structure because it stores information using names.

Objects Use Curly Braces

{ }

The entire group of information inside the curly braces is one object.

Objects store information using key-value pairs.

key: value

What Is a Key?

The key is the name used to identify a piece of information.

For example:

name: "Alex"

Here, name is the key.

What Is a Value?

The value is the information stored under that key.

name: "Alex"

Here, "Alex" is the value.

You can think of an object like a list where every item has a label.

Array
↓
["Alex", "alex@example.com", 18]

Object
↓
{
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  age: 18
}

The object is easier to understand because every value has a meaningful name.

Creating an Object

const customer = {
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  age: 18
};

Now customer contains three named pieces of information.

Reading a Value

We can access an object's values using the key.

console.log(customer.name);
console.log(customer.email);
console.log(customer.age);

The dot means we want to access a property of the object.

We can also use bracket notation:

console.log(customer["name"]);

Both approaches can access the same property.

Adding a New Property

Objects can gain new properties after they are created.

customer.address = "Davao";

Now the object also contains an address property.

Editing a Property

We can assign a new value to an existing key:

customer.age = 19;

The customer's age is now 19.

Removing a Property

We can use the delete operator to remove a property.

delete customer.address;

The address property is removed from the object.

Keys Should Be Unique Within the Object

An object should not rely on having multiple properties with the same key.

const customer = {
  name: "Alex",
  name: "Jamie"
};

This does not create two separate name properties that JavaScript can independently distinguish. The later definition replaces the earlier one.

Think of the key as the label on a drawer.

Within the same object, you should not create two drawers with the exact same label and expect JavaScript to know which one you mean.

Multiple Objects Can Exist

The fact that keys should be unique inside one object does not mean your entire program can only have one object.

You can create many objects:

const customer1 = {
  name: "Alex"
};

const customer2 = {
  name: "Jamie"
};

Both objects can have a name key because they are separate objects.

Why Objects Matter for Sign Up

One user account can naturally be represented by an object:

const user = {
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "example123"
};

This is much easier to understand than an array where we have to remember which index means which piece of information.

Try It

Create an object representing a customer. Give it a name, email, age, and another property of your choice. Read each property with dot notation. Add a new property. Edit one property. Delete one property. Then create a second customer object with some of the same property names.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Arrays and Objects Together
Contents.Contents:
So Why Did We Learn Both?

You now know two different ways to organize information.

Array
↓
Stores multiple items

Object
↓
Stores named information about one item

On their own, both are useful.

Together, they become extremely powerful.

Our POS Already Gives Us the Perfect Example

Think about the products in our POS application.

A product needs more than just a name.

We might need:

Name
Price
Category
Stock

An object is a good way to describe one product:

{
  name: "Burger",
  price: 85
}

But our POS does not have only one product.

It has many products.

That means we can use an array containing many product objects.

const products = [
  {name: "Burger", price: 85},
  {name: "Pizza", price: 120},
  {name: "Fries", price: 55},
  {name: "Hotdog", price: 45},
  {name: "Chicken", price: 110}
];

Read One Product

Because products is an array, we use an index to select one product.

console.log(products[0]);

The result is an object representing the Burger.

Read a Property From That Product

Now we can combine array indexing with object property access.

console.log(products[0].name);
console.log(products[0].price);

The first part:

products[0]

selects the first object.

The second part:

.name

selects the name property from that object.

The Same Idea With Multiple Products

products[1].name
products[2].price
products[4].name

This allows one array to contain many objects while each object contains its own named information.

Arrays Can Contain Objects

This is one of the most important patterns for our project.

[
  { ... },
  { ... },
  { ... }
]

The square brackets tell us we are looking at an array.

The curly braces inside tell us that each item is an object.

Objects Can Also Contain Arrays

The relationship can work in the other direction too.

An object can have an array as one of its values.

const customer = {
  name: "Alex",
  favoriteFoods: [
    "Pizza",
    "Burger",
    "Fries"
  ]
};

Now we have:

customer.name
customer.favoriteFoods
customer.favoriteFoods[0]

The last expression gets the first item from the array stored inside the object.

Arrays Can Contain Arrays

An array can also contain another array.

const groups = [
  ["Alex", "Jamie"],
  ["Sam", "Taylor"]
];

Now:

groups[0]

gives us the first inner array.

And:

groups[0][1]

gets the second item from that inner array.

Objects Can Contain Objects

An object can also contain another object as a value.

const user = {
  name: "Alex",
  address: {
    city: "Davao",
    country: "Philippines"
  }
};

We can then access nested properties:

user.address.city
user.address.country

This is called nested data.

Why Is Nested Data Useful?

Real applications rarely store everything in one flat value.

Information often has relationships.

A customer can have orders.

An order can have products.

A product can have a category.

A user can have account information.

Arrays and objects allow us to represent these relationships.

Now Think About Users

We can apply the same idea to Sign Up.

One user can be represented as an object:

{
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "example123"
}

Many users can then be stored inside an array:

const users = [
  {
    name: "Alex",
    email: "alex@example.com",
    password: "example123"
  },
  {
    name: "Jamie",
    email: "jamie@example.com",
    password: "hello123"
  }
];

Now we have a very simple representation of multiple accounts.

Finding a User

Later, JavaScript can search through this array and find a user whose email matches what someone entered during Login.

We are not implementing that yet.

The important idea is understanding the data structure first.

The Pattern to Remember

Object
↓
Describes one thing

Array
↓
Stores many things

Array + Object
↓
Stores many things
with named information about each one

Try It

Create an array containing at least three objects. Make each object describe a person, product, game character, or something else you choose. Give each object at least three properties. Then read values using both an array index and an object key. Create one nested object, one object containing an array, and one array containing another array. Use console.log() to inspect the results.

Contents.Title: Checkpoint: Prepare for Sign-Up
Contents.Contents:
Now We Have the Data Structures We Need

We have not built Sign-Up functionality yet.

Instead, we have learned the structures that will make it possible.

We learned:

  • variables can store individual values
  • arrays can store multiple items
  • indexes allow us to access array items
  • arrays can grow and shrink
  • objects store named information using key-value pairs
  • object properties can be read, added, edited, and removed
  • arrays and objects can be combined
  • data can be nested inside other data

The Structure We Will Eventually Use

users
↓
Array
↓
Multiple user objects
↓
Each object contains:
name
email
password

That structure gives us a much better foundation for Sign Up than simply keeping one fixed username and password.

Why Did We Stop Here?

Because there is an important programming principle behind this lesson:

Understand how the data is organized before writing the logic that changes it.

Once we start implementing Sign Up, JavaScript will need to:

Read the Sign-Up form
↓
Create a user object
↓
Add the object to an array
↓
Store the updated data
↓
Later allow Login to find the user

Now you know what each of those pieces means.

Try It

Before continuing to Sign-Up functionality, create your own users array containing several example user objects. Give each user a name, email, and password. Read different users and properties using indexes and keys. Add a new user and remove one. Make sure you can explain why an array is being used for the collection and an object is being used for each individual user.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Now We Build Sign-Up Functionality
Contents.Contents:
From Learning About Data to Building Sign Up

We have reached the point where the concepts we learned about arrays and objects finally have a purpose.

Earlier, we completed the basic Sign-In functionality. That lesson taught us how JavaScript can read information from a form, compare values, make a decision, and display the result.

We also created the Sign-Up interface earlier while learning HTML and CSS. The form already exists, and now JavaScript will give it behavior.

Remember Our Two Forms

Sign-In
├── Email
├── Password
└── Login

Sign-Up
├── Name
├── Email
├── Password
├── Confirm Password
└── Sign Up

The Sign-In form asks:

"Does this account's information match?"

The Sign-Up form asks:

"Can we create a new account from this information?"

Why Do We Need More Than One Account?

Our earlier Sign-In lesson used one fixed email and password because the goal was to learn the basic comparison logic.

But an application may have many users.

That means we need somewhere to keep multiple accounts.

This is exactly why we learned:

Object
↓
Describes one user

Array
↓
Stores many users

Array + Object
↓
Stores many users with their information

The Sign-Up Process

User fills in Sign-Up form
↓
JavaScript reads the values
↓
JavaScript checks the values
↓
Create a user object
↓
Add it to the users array
↓
Save the updated users
↓
Account now exists
↓
Sign-In can find it later

This is the connection between the lessons we have already completed and the new functionality we are about to build.

Try It

Open the same project you used for Sign-In. Switch to the Sign-Up view and look at the four existing inputs. Do not create a separate webpage. We are continuing the same project and adding JavaScript behavior to the existing Sign-Up interface.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Find the Sign-Up Form
Contents.Contents:
JavaScript Needs to Find the Sign-Up Form

Before JavaScript can react to Sign Up, it needs a reference to the form.

Our existing HTML already has an ID for the form:

<form id="signupForm">

We can find it with getElementById(), just as we did with the Sign-In form.

const signupForm =
  document.getElementById("signupForm");

Compare This With Sign-In

Sign-In:
const loginForm =
  document.getElementById("loginForm");

Sign-Up:
const signupForm =
  document.getElementById("signupForm");

The idea is exactly the same.

The only difference is which HTML element JavaScript needs to control.

Find the Sign-Up Inputs

Our existing Sign-Up HTML already gives each input an ID:

signupName
signupEmail
signupPassword
signupConfirm

JavaScript can find each one:

const signupName =
  document.getElementById("signupName");

const signupEmail =
  document.getElementById("signupEmail");

const signupPassword =
  document.getElementById("signupPassword");

const signupConfirm =
  document.getElementById("signupConfirm");

Notice that the variable names do not have to be identical to the IDs. What matters is the text inside getElementById().

The Message Element

We also have:

<div id="signupMessage"></div>

JavaScript can find that too:

const signupMessage =
  document.getElementById("signupMessage");

This is where we will eventually display messages such as:

Passwords do not match.

Account created successfully.

Why Are These IDs Important?

HTML ID
↓
getElementById()
↓
JavaScript reference
↓
JavaScript can work with the element

Try It

Use getElementById() to find signupForm, signupName, signupEmail, signupPassword, signupConfirm, and signupMessage. Use console.log() while practicing so you can inspect the references.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Listen for Sign-Up Submission
Contents.Contents:
Wait for the User to Create an Account

Finding the Sign-Up form is only the beginning. JavaScript also needs to know when the user submits it.

Just like Sign-In, we use the submit event.

signupForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {
    // Sign-Up code goes here
  }
);

Compare It With Sign-In

loginForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {
    // Login code
  }
);
signupForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {
    // Sign-Up code
  }
);

The pattern is the same. JavaScript waits for the user to submit a particular form and then runs the function.

Prevent the Normal Submission

We also need the same preventDefault() behavior that we used in Sign-In.

signupForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {

    event.preventDefault();

  }
);

Now the browser will not immediately perform its normal form submission behavior. JavaScript gets control of the process.

The Sign-Up Flow So Far

User clicks Sign Up
↓
Form submits
↓
JavaScript receives the submit event
↓
event.preventDefault()
↓
JavaScript handles Sign Up

Try It

Add the submit listener to your Sign-Up form and call event.preventDefault(). Submit the form and observe that the page stays where it is.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Read the Sign-Up Values
Contents.Contents:
Get the Information the User Entered

Now JavaScript knows when the Sign-Up form is submitted. The next step is to read the information inside it.

Our form has four values:

Name
Email
Password
Confirm Password

Read the Name

const name =
  document
    .getElementById("signupName")
    .value
    .trim();

The .value property gives us what the user entered.

The .trim() method removes whitespace from the beginning and end of the text.

Read the Email

const email =
  document
    .getElementById("signupEmail")
    .value
    .trim();

Read the Password

const password =
  document
    .getElementById("signupPassword")
    .value;

Read the Confirmation

const confirm =
  document
    .getElementById("signupConfirm")
    .value;

Now We Have Four Variables

name
email
password
confirm

These variables contain the values that were entered into the Sign-Up form.

Compare This With Sign-In

Sign-In only needed two values:

email
password

Sign-Up needs more information because it is creating an account instead of checking an existing login.

Sign-In
↓
Read email
↓
Read password

Sign-Up
↓
Read name
↓
Read email
↓
Read password
↓
Read confirmation

Try It

Read all four Sign-Up values in your submit listener. Temporarily use console.log() to inspect the values while learning and make sure JavaScript is reading the correct inputs.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Check the Password Confirmation
Contents.Contents:
Make Sure the Passwords Match

We now have the user's password and the repeated confirmation password.

Before creating the account, we should make sure they are identical.

Compare the Two Values

password === confirm

This asks whether the password and confirmation are exactly the same.

We can use if to react when they are different.

if (password !== confirm) {
  // passwords are different
}

The !== operator means not strictly equal.

Show the User What Happened

Our Sign-Up interface already contains:

<div id="signupMessage"></div>

JavaScript can change its text using textContent.

signupMessage.textContent =
  "Passwords do not match.";

Stop the Process

If the passwords do not match, there is no reason to continue creating the account.

We can use return to stop the current function.

if (password !== confirm) {

  signupMessage.textContent =
    "Passwords do not match.";

  return;
}

This means:

Passwords different?
↓
Show error
↓
Stop here

Why Is This Similar to Sign-In?

Our Sign-In lesson also used if to decide what should happen.

Sign-In
↓
Credentials match?
↓
Yes → continue
No → show error

Sign-Up uses the same programming idea:

Sign-Up
↓
Passwords match?
↓
Yes → continue
No → show error

Try It

Make the Sign-Up form display Passwords do not match. when the two password fields contain different values. Test both matching and non-matching passwords.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Check the Password Length
Contents.Contents:
Check Another Requirement

Our Sign-Up HTML already uses the minlength attribute:

<input
  id="signupPassword"
  type="password"
  minlength="6"
  required
>

This tells the browser that the password should contain at least six characters.

We can also understand the same rule through JavaScript.

Using .length

Strings have a length property.

password.length

For example:

"hello".length

has the value:

5

Check the Password

if (password.length < 6) {

  signupMessage.textContent =
    "Password must be at least 6 characters.";

  return;
}

The condition asks whether the password contains fewer than six characters.

Why Check It With JavaScript?

HTML validation can prevent the form from being submitted when the requirement is not satisfied.

JavaScript gives us additional control over what our program does after the submission begins.

At this stage, the important lesson is not about making the validation perfectly secure. It is about understanding how JavaScript can inspect a value and make a decision from it.

Our Validation So Far

Read the form
↓
Are the passwords equal?
↓
No → Show message and stop
↓
Yes
↓
Is the password at least 6 characters?
↓
No → Show message and stop
↓
Yes → Continue

Try It

Add the password-length check after the password-confirmation check. Test a short password and then a valid password. Observe which branch JavaScript takes.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Create the New User Object
Contents.Contents:
Turn the Form Values Into a User

We have now read the Sign-Up form and checked the basic requirements.

The next step is to create something that represents the new account.

This is where the object lesson becomes useful.

One User Is an Object

const user = {
  name,
  email,
  password
};

This creates one object containing the user's information.

Why Don't We Store confirm?

confirm was used to make sure the user typed the same password twice.

Once that check succeeds, the confirmation value does not need to become part of the account.

The account only needs:

name
email
password

Think About Our POS Example

Remember the product objects we studied:

{
  name: "Burger",
  price: 85
}

That object describes one product.

Our new object describes one user:

{
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "example123"
}

The idea is identical: an object groups related information and gives each value a meaningful property name.

Why Is This Better Than Separate Variables?

We could keep:

name
email
password

as separate values, but the object gives them one clear identity:

user

Now we can think of the entire account as one value.

Try It

Create the user object from your Sign-Up variables. Use console.log(user) to inspect it. Then access its properties with user.name, user.email, and user.password.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Store Multiple Users in an Array
Contents.Contents:
One User Is Not Enough

We now know how to represent one account using an object.

But our original reason for learning arrays was that an application may have many users.

So we need to combine the two structures.

One User

const user = {
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "example123"
};

Many Users

We can place user objects inside an array:

const users = [
  {
    name: "Alex",
    email: "alex@example.com",
    password: "example123"
  },
  {
    name: "Jamie",
    email: "jamie@example.com",
    password: "hello123"
  }
];

The Pattern

users
↓
Array
↓
User object
↓
name
email
password

This is exactly the pattern we learned earlier with the POS products.

products
↓
Array
↓
Product object
↓
name
price

Adding a New User

Because users is an array, we can use push().

users.push(user);

The new user object is added to the end of the array.

What Happens After Sign Up?

Existing users
↓
[ user1, user2, user3 ]

New Sign-Up
↓
create user4

users.push(user4)
↓
[ user1, user2, user3, user4 ]

This is the basic structure needed for multiple accounts.

Why Can't We Just Replace the Old User?

Because that would mean each new Sign-Up would destroy the previous account.

We need a collection that can keep all of the accounts.

Try It

Create a users array containing two example users. Create another user object and add it with push(). Use console.log(users) to observe that all of the objects remain in the array.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Start With an Empty Users Array
Contents.Contents:
Our Real Application Should Start Without Fake Users

During the previous lesson we used example users to understand the structure.

For the actual Sign-Up system, we want the application to begin with a collection that can receive new accounts.

const users = [];

This creates an empty array.

What Does [] Mean?

The square brackets represent an array.

Because there is nothing between them, the array currently contains no items.

[]
↓
No users yet

Adding the First User

When someone signs up, we create a user object and add it:

users.push(user);

Now the array changes from:

[]

to something like:

[
  {
    name: "Alex",
    email: "alex@example.com",
    password: "example123"
  }
]

Adding Another User

A second Sign-Up does not erase the first user.

It adds another object:

[
  { name: "Alex", ... },
  { name: "Jamie", ... }
]

Why Is This Important?

Now the Sign-Up form can create accounts instead of replacing one fixed credential.

This is the first major difference between our earlier Sign-In example and the new system.

Earlier Sign-In lesson
↓
One fixed account

New system
↓
Array of user objects
↓
Many accounts

One Important Problem

There is still a problem with using only:

const users = [];

If the page is refreshed, the JavaScript starts again and the array becomes empty again.

We need a way to save the array.

Try It

Create an empty users array. Add several example user objects with push(). Refresh the page and observe that ordinary JavaScript variables do not automatically preserve the array.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Save Users With localStorage
Contents.Contents:
Keep the Accounts After Refreshing the Page

We discovered an important problem: a normal JavaScript array exists only while the current page is running.

For our learning project, we can use the browser's localStorage to keep the user data between page loads.

What Is localStorage?

localStorage is browser storage that allows a webpage to save string data and retrieve it later.

We can save a value with:

localStorage.setItem("users", "some value");

The first argument is the key.

The second argument is the string value we want to save.

But Our Users Array Is Not a String

Our users array contains objects:

const users = [
  {
    name: "Alex",
    email: "alex@example.com",
    password: "example123"
  }
];

We can convert that JavaScript value into a JSON string with JSON.stringify().

localStorage.setItem(
  "users",
  JSON.stringify(users)
);

Reading the Saved Data

To retrieve the value later, we use:

localStorage.getItem("users");

The result is a string, so we use JSON.parse() to turn it back into JavaScript data.

const savedUsers =
  JSON.parse(
    localStorage.getItem("users")
  );

The Complete Conversion

JavaScript array
↓
JSON.stringify()
↓
String
↓
localStorage

localStorage
↓
String
↓
JSON.parse()
↓
JavaScript array

Why Is This Connected to Sign-In?

Because Sign-Up creates the account, while Sign-In needs to retrieve the account later.

Sign-Up
↓
Create user
↓
Add user to users array
↓
Save users array

Sign-In
↓
Load users array
↓
Search for matching user
↓
Compare credentials

Important Learning Note

This browser-storage system is intentionally simple for learning. It is not a secure production authentication system, and passwords should not be stored as plain text in a real application.

Try It

Create a small users array, save it with JSON.stringify(), refresh the page, and load it again using JSON.parse(). Use console.log() to inspect the restored array.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Load the Existing Users
Contents.Contents:
The Application Needs to Remember Existing Accounts

We now know how to save users, but the application also needs to load those users when the page starts.

Otherwise, every refresh would start with an empty collection.

Get the Saved Value

const savedUsers =
  localStorage.getItem("users");

There are two possible situations.

Saved data exists
↓
Load it

No saved data
↓
Start with an empty array

Use an if Statement

let users = [];

const savedUsers =
  localStorage.getItem("users");

if (savedUsers) {
  users = JSON.parse(savedUsers);
}

We use let here because the variable may receive the saved array later.

Why Not Just Write const users = []?

If we declare the array with const, we can still add and remove items from it, but we cannot replace the entire array with a different array.

For this particular initialization pattern, using let makes the reassignment clear:

let users = [];
users = JSON.parse(savedUsers);

The Result

First visit
↓
No saved users
↓
users = []

Later visit
↓
Saved users found
↓
JSON.parse()
↓
users contains previous accounts

Why This Matters for Sign Up

Now a new Sign-Up does not have to start from an empty collection every time.

The application can load the accounts that were created previously and then add the new one.

Try It

Write the initialization code for users. Save a few users, reload the page, and use console.log(users) to verify that the previous accounts were loaded.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Check Whether the Email Already Exists
Contents.Contents:
Prevent Duplicate Accounts

Our Sign-Up system can now create users, but there is another important question.

What happens if someone tries to create another account using an email address that already exists?

We should check before adding the new user.

We Need to Search the Users

Our users are stored in an array:

users = [
  { email: "alex@example.com", ... },
  { email: "jamie@example.com", ... }
];

We need to determine whether any object already has the entered email.

Use find()

JavaScript provides the find() method for searching an array and returning the first item that matches a condition.

const existingUser =
  users.find(
    user => user.email === email
  );

JavaScript checks the users one at a time.

user.email === email

If a matching user is found, existingUser will contain that object.

If no matching user exists, the result will be undefined.

Use the Result

if (existingUser) {

  signupMessage.textContent =
    "An account with this email already exists.";

  return;
}

Now the new account is only created when the email is not already in the array.

Why Is This Important?

The email becomes a way to distinguish accounts.

Existing account?
↓
Yes → Stop Sign Up

No → Create the new account

Connection to Our Earlier Lessons

This single example combines several concepts we already learned:

Array
↓
find()
↓
Object property
↓
=== comparison
↓
if statement

We are no longer learning isolated pieces. We are combining them into a real program.

Try It

Create several user objects with different email addresses. Use find() to search for an email. Test both a matching email and an email that does not exist.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Add the New User to the Array
Contents.Contents:
Now We Can Actually Create the Account

At this point, JavaScript has:

1. Read the Sign-Up form
2. Checked the password confirmation
3. Checked the password length
4. Checked whether the email already exists
5. Created the user object

There is only one major step left: add the new user to the collection.

Use push()

users.push(user);

The user object is now added to the end of the users array.

Save the Updated Array

Adding the user to the array changes the JavaScript data, but we also need to update the saved copy.

localStorage.setItem(
  "users",
  JSON.stringify(users)
);

The Complete Creation Sequence

Sign-Up submitted
↓
Read form values
↓
Validate information
↓
Check duplicate email
↓
Create user object
↓
users.push(user)
↓
JSON.stringify(users)
↓
localStorage.setItem("users", ...)
↓
Account saved

What Happens to the Array?

Suppose the array originally contains:

[
  {name: "Alex", email: "alex@example.com"},
  {name: "Jamie", email: "jamie@example.com"}
]

After:

users.push(user);

it might become:

[
  {name: "Alex", email: "alex@example.com"},
  {name: "Jamie", email: "jamie@example.com"},
  {name: "Sam", email: "sam@example.com"}
]

The earlier accounts remain. The new account is simply added to the collection.

Why Is This the Core of Sign Up?

Creating an account is ultimately the process of taking the user's information and adding a new account to the collection of existing accounts.

Try It

Add a new user object to your users array with push(). Then save the updated array to localStorage. Create more than one account and inspect the stored data to see that the accounts remain together.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Display the Sign-Up Result
Contents.Contents:
Tell the User That the Account Was Created

The account has now been added and saved, but the person using the webpage needs feedback.

Our Sign-Up interface already contains a message area:

<div id="signupMessage"></div>

We can use textContent to tell the user what happened.

Success Message

signupMessage.style.color =
  "var(--success)";

signupMessage.textContent =
  "Account created. You can now login.";

Error Messages

We can use the same element for errors:

signupMessage.style.color =
  "var(--danger)";

signupMessage.textContent =
  "Passwords do not match.";

The message area can therefore communicate both successful and unsuccessful Sign-Up attempts.

Sign-Up Feedback

Success
↓
Account created. You can now login.

Failure
↓
Explain why Sign Up could not continue

Connecting This to Sign-In

Our Sign-In lesson taught us that the webpage itself should show the result to the user.

The same principle applies here.

Sign-In
↓
loginMessage.textContent

Sign-Up
↓
signupMessage.textContent

Both forms use the DOM to provide visible feedback.

Try It

Display a success message after creating an account. Also display messages for invalid passwords and duplicate emails. Test each situation and observe how the same message element changes.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Return the User to Sign-In
Contents.Contents:
Sign Up and Sign In Should Work Together

Creating an account is useful, but the user will usually want to sign in after creating it.

Our existing interface already contains both views:

loginView
signupView

The Login and Sign-Up switch buttons already exist in the HTML.

After Successful Sign Up

Once the account has been created successfully, we can switch back to the Sign-In view.

signupView.style.display = "none";
loginView.style.display = "block";

We can also place the newly created email into the Login email field:

document
  .getElementById("loginEmail")
  .value = email;

Now the user does not have to type their email again.

Think About the User Experience

Sign Up
↓
Account created
↓
Return to Login
↓
Email already filled in
↓
User enters password
↓
Login

This connects the two views into one continuous process.

Why Not Automatically Log In?

For this lesson, we are keeping the steps separate so you can clearly understand the relationship between account creation and account checking.

Sign Up creates the account.

Sign In checks the account.

Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the programming logic easier to understand.

Try It

After successful Sign Up, switch the interface back to Login and place the newly entered email into the Login email input. Test the complete flow from Sign Up to Login.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Replace the Fixed Login With Real Users
Contents.Contents:
Now Sign-In Can Use the Accounts We Created

This is the important connection between our two lessons.

Earlier, Sign-In used fixed credentials:

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";
const correctPassword = "1234";

That worked for learning the basic comparison logic, but it only represented one account.

We now have a collection of users.

users = [
  {
    name: "Alex",
    email: "alex@example.com",
    password: "example123"
  },
  {
    name: "Jamie",
    email: "jamie@example.com",
    password: "hello123"
  }
];

Find the User During Login

Instead of comparing the entered email with one fixed value, we can search the users array.

const user = users.find(
  user => user.email === email
);

JavaScript looks through the users array and tries to find an account whose email matches the entered email.

What If No User Exists?

if (!user) {

  loginMessage.textContent =
    "No account found.";

  return;
}

The ! means not.

So !user means there is no matching user object.

Now Check the Password

if (password !== user.password) {

  loginMessage.textContent =
    "Invalid email or password.";

  return;
}

If the email was found but the password does not match, Login fails.

Successful Login

loginMessage.textContent =
  "Login successful!";

The New Authentication Flow

Sign Up
↓
Create user object
↓
Add to users array
↓
Save users

Sign In
↓
Load users
↓
Find matching email
↓
Check password
↓
Login succeeds or fails

This is a major step forward from the fixed-credential example.

Important Note

This is still a learning authentication system. The browser storage and plain-text password handling are not appropriate for real production authentication.

Try It

Update your Sign-In logic so it searches the users array instead of using correctEmail and correctPassword. Create two accounts through Sign Up and test signing in with each account.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Put Sign-Up and Sign-In Together
Contents.Contents:
We Now Have One Connected Authentication Example

We started with two separate ideas:

Sign-In
↓
Check fixed credentials

Sign-Up
↓
Learn arrays and objects

Now those ideas can become one connected system.

Sign-Up Creates Accounts

Read Sign-Up form
↓
Validate information
↓
Create user object
↓
Add object to users array
↓
Save users

Sign-In Uses Those Accounts

Read Login form
↓
Load users
↓
Find matching email
↓
Check password
↓
Display result

The Shared Data

The most important connection is the users array.

Sign Up
     ↓
  users array
     ↑
     │
Sign In

Sign Up adds accounts to the collection.

Sign In reads from the same collection.

That means the two forms are finally working with the same account data.

Why Did We Learn Arrays and Objects First?

Without understanding arrays and objects, the account system would seem like a complicated block of code.

Now we can explain each layer:

Object
↓
One user

Array
↓
Many users

localStorage
↓
Keep the users between page loads

Sign-Up
↓
Adds users

Sign-In
↓
Finds users

This Is Still a Learning Project

We are intentionally keeping the system simple enough to understand.

A real authentication system should not trust browser JavaScript or store passwords as plain text. Real applications use server-side authentication and secure password handling.

For this course, however, the important goal is understanding how the parts connect.

Try It

Create at least two accounts through Sign Up. Then return to Login and test each account separately. Also test an incorrect password and an email that does not exist. Make sure you can explain how the users array connects Sign-Up and Sign-In.

Contents.Title: Final Checkpoint: Build Sign Up Yourself
Contents.Contents:
Now Rebuild the Sign-Up Functionality

You have now learned the pieces required to make the Sign-Up interface functional.

Do not think of the completed code as one giant program. Break it into the ideas you have already learned.

Build in This Order

  1. Find the Sign-Up form using getElementById().
  2. Listen for the form's submit event.
  3. Use event.preventDefault().
  4. Read the name, email, password, and confirmation values.
  5. Check whether the passwords match.
  6. Check the password length.
  7. Load the existing users array.
  8. Check whether the email is already being used.
  9. Create a user object.
  10. Add the user object with push().
  11. Save the updated users array with JSON.stringify() and localStorage.
  12. Display a success message using textContent.
  13. Return the user to the Sign-In view.
  14. Update Sign-In so it searches the users array instead of using fixed credentials.

The Complete Relationship

HTML
↓
Creates Sign-In and Sign-Up

CSS
↓
Makes both interfaces look good

JavaScript
↓
Controls both forms
↓
Creates user objects
↓
Stores users in an array
↓
Saves the array
↓
Sign-In searches the array

Things You Should Be Able to Explain

Why does the Sign-Up form need an ID?

Why do the Sign-Up inputs have IDs?

Why do we use addEventListener()?

Why do we use event.preventDefault()?

What does .value give us?

Why do we use an object for one user?

Why do we use an array for multiple users?

What does push() do?

Why do we use JSON.stringify()?

Why do we use JSON.parse()?

Why do we use localStorage?

Why should the email be checked before creating another account?

How does Sign-Up communicate with Sign-In through the shared users array?

Final Practice

Build the Sign-Up functionality yourself using the concepts from the previous lessons. Create multiple accounts. Try creating an account with the same email twice. Try mismatched passwords. Try a short password. Then sign in using each account you created.

The goal is no longer to memorize code. The goal is to understand the chain:

Form
↓
Values
↓
Validation
↓
Object
↓
Array
↓
Storage
↓
Sign In

Once you can explain that chain, you have connected the Sign-Up lessons directly to the Sign-In system you built earlier.
